thread.title: Half of Americans struggle to afford food, LendingTree survey finds
thread.title_full: Half of Americans struggle to afford food, LendingTree survey finds

author: d. m. priest
title: Half of Americans struggle to afford food, LendingTree survey finds
text:
Half of Americans are struggling to afford food, with a majority experiencing food anxiety, according to research released by LendingTree on Mar. 26. The findings come from a survey of 2,000 U.S. consumers conducted in February.
The report highlights the growing impact of rising food prices on American households. According to the data, six in ten people have worried about paying for groceries in the past month. Younger generations, parents with young children, and low-income households are especially affected by these concerns.
LendingTree found that most people are changing how they shop for groceries (86%) and eat at restaurants (84%) in an effort to minimize costs. Strategies include paying closer attention to grocery prices, cutting back on splurge items and waste, choosing generic brands, creating shopping lists and using more coupons.
More than half (52%) said they’re spending more on food than last year; nearly half say it’s at least somewhat difficult to afford food now. Certain groups feel this squeeze most: 19% of Generation Z adults (ages 18-29), 18% of millennials (30-45), 17% of parents with young kids and 22% of those in low-income households report that affording food has become very difficult. Baby boomers are least likely to report hardship.
Food anxiety is widespread even among higher-income groups—57% with household incomes above $100,000 reported concern about paying for groceries recently. Meanwhile, debit cards remain the most popular payment method for groceries overall; high-income shoppers are almost twice as likely as low-income shoppers to use grocery rewards credit cards.
Dining habits have also shifted: while four out of ten Americans still eat out or order takeout weekly or more often—and high earners do so more frequently—many have cut back due to cost pressures. About two in five respondents say they’re eating out less; others choose cheaper restaurants or tip less frequently than before.
LendingTree said that inflation has changed tipping habits for most Americans (66%), particularly among younger generations who now tip less often or not at all for takeout and delivery orders. Still, some groups—including millennials and parents—are among the most likely to increase their tips despite financial stress.
The survey was conducted online between Feb. 4-10 using quotas designed to reflect national demographics.
